item.title: My body. My pregnancy. - Between anxiety and anticipation | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Being pregnant is a profound experience. How does it affect the body and mind? What counts as a high-risk pregnancy? How does stress affect the baby? Anticipation and worry go hand in hand.
The film follows three women through their pregnancies. Young city-dweller Assia is expecting her first child. On the one hand, she is full of anticipation and optimism. At the same time, she struggles with the physical changes that come with pregnancy. Tamara is already a mother. She is expecting twins and her pregnancy is therefore considered to be high-risk. To avoid premature labor, she has to take it easy - a challenge for her. The documentary also follows the pregnant Kathy. After longing for a child for a long time, she suddenly became pregnant "just like that.” She faces many fears and worries until she finally holds her baby in her arms.
The documentary provides a scientifically grounded look at how closely mother and child are connected - and how a baby changes not only the body, but a person’s entire life.

item.title: How the Iran war accidentally boosted clean energy | The Gray Area
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
Could a war that disrupted the world’s oil supply end up accelerating the shift away from it?
Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO
In today’s episode, Vox senior reporter and producer Miles Bryan talks with Jason Bordoff, founding director of Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy and a former Obama energy adviser, about an unintended upside of the Iran war: the impact on global energy consumption. They explore why energy security can motivate change where climate warnings haven’t, how China is poised to take advantage of this moment, and whether the US risks getting left behind.
The war in Iran has given countries a powerful reason to embrace green energy: protecting themselves from the next oil shock. Solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles aren’t just tools for fighting climate change. They’re increasingly a way to secure affordable energy in a world where a distant conflict can upend daily life. But the same search for cheap, reliable power is also driving investment in coal, oil, and gas, raising the question of how much this crisis will actually change.

item.title: How China’s Export Machine Is Beating Tariffs
item.author: Bloomberg Originals
item.content:encoded:
Tariffs and trade barriers thrown up by the US and Europe were supposed to slow China’s export machine. Instead, it has accelerated. China’s trade surplus this year is on track to exceed the $1.2 trillion record set in 2025.
While China’s exports to the West dropped between 2024 and 2025, its exports to Southeast Asia, South and Central America, Africa, Japan and South Korea all increased. And it’s not only about finding new markets abroad: China also has moved up the value chain. The country is now a major force in everything from electric cars and solar panels to robots and artificial intelligence.
But China’s export boom is unfolding against a fragile domestic backdrop. The country continues to grapple with weak consumer demand, a prolonged property downturn and high youth unemployment, making exports an increasingly important source of growth.

item.title: Paris's Hidden Egyptian Temple? Investigating Secret Occult Symbols Across Europe
item.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
item.content:encoded: A pyramid in Paris, a claimed 666 panes of glass, and a president who visited it at night. What was really built into the heart of the City of Light? From Saint-Sulpice’s concealed figure clutching forbidden scrolls to the Louvre’s pyramid aligned like Giza, we trace claims of Masonic design across Paris. Why did François Mitterrand seed obelisks and arches along a Luxor-like axis? And what do the Bilderberg meetings, the All-Seeing Eye, and pop culture symbols actually prove—or not? Then to London: Hawksmoor’s churches mapped as a pentagram, St Paul’s placed as a new Solomon’s Temple, and the Ripper murders plotted into a ritual shape. Are these alignments evidence of a hidden network, or are we connecting dots that were never meant to meet? We weigh myth against records—from Adam Weishaupt’s 1776 society to “God’s Banker” Roberto Calvi—and ask what survives today: a cabal, a culture, or just a captivating story. item.title: Jellyfish - The ocean's new rulers? | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Jellyfish have been around for more than 500 million years. They don't have a heart, a brain or a skeleton, and are 90 percent water. But the damage they're able to inflict often makes the headlines.
Despite an apparently basic physical makeup, they possess remarkable abilities. Some species are highly poisonous, whereas others are considered virtually immortal. Will jellyfish become the future rulers of the seas?
Their long evolutionary history means jellyfish are now present in all the world's oceans. But their growing prevalence poses challenges for both people and the natural world: They sting bathers, disrupt the cooling systems of power stations and threaten fisheries and aquaculture.
For decades now, jellyfish blooms in the Mediterranean, in the Norwegian fjords and off the coast of Namibia have been occurring with increasing frequency, altering marine ecosystems and displacing fish. These creatures benefit from characteristics that make them exceptional survivors.
They've outlived the dinosaurs. In our ever-changing marine environment, could jellyfish also emerge again as the great survivors?

item.title: Congo's blood minerals - The high price of high-tech | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Without coltan, the digital world would grind to a halt. The coveted mineral is used in cellphones, computers and countless other high-tech products.
The consequences of the world's hunger for raw materials are particularly visible in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. A significant share of the world's coltan is mined there. Consumers around the globe benefit from modern technology, with its supply chain that can often be traced back to the Kivu region and its mines. Armed groups there fight for control over the lucrative deposits. The men, women and children that mine the coveted ore often do so under threat, and in life-threatening conditions. Covert trading networks deliver coltan to the global market. This documentary follows the mineral's journey and exposes the mechanisms of a system in which natural-resource wealth, violence and economic interest are closely interwoven.

item.title: How US intervention is changing Venezuela
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
In the days after the military operation that ousted Nicolás Maduro, a poll from the Caracas‑based firm Meganálisis showed that 92% of Venezuelans were grateful to President Donald Trump for removing Maduro and that 90% wanted the US as Venezuela’s main ally. During the months since, the US has been heavily involved in shaping Venezuela’s future. But some key reforms are moving slower than Venezuelans hoped for.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a three-step plan for US intervention in Venezuela: stability, recovery, and a transition to democracy. While plans for political reforms and democratic elections in Venezuela are moving slowly, the designs for who controls its oil have been moving fast. The US recently announced an agreement with Venezuela as “the biggest oil deal in world history.”
As Venezuelans hold out hope that the final step in Rubio’s plan, a transition to democracy, will still materialize, support among Venezuelans for Trump appears to be slipping. According to a new Meganálisis poll, 83% of Venezuelans don’t believe Trump wants what is best for their country. As voices grow louder from opposition leaders like Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado to jumpstart democratic processes, pressure on the US is mounting to make good on their promise.
Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains, that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the events that led to Maduro’s ousting, the lingering discord between the Venezuelan government and its people, and how US intervention is shaping the country’s future.

More than 16 years after it was signed into law, the Affordable Care Act — also known as “Obamacare” — is still a flashpoint in American life and politics. “Obama’s Deal,” a FRONTLINE documentary that’s now available to stream on YouTube for the first time, tells the story of how this historic — and controversial — piece of legislation was passed.
In the documentary, veteran FRONTLINE producer Michael Kirk and his team took viewers behind the headlines and revealed the political maneuvering behind the healthcare reform bill’s passage, along party lines, in March 2010.
The passage followed a bruising year of debate, negotiation and backlash. Through interviews with administration officials, senators and Washington lobbyists, “Obama’s Deal” traced the dramatic details of how an idealistic president pursued the health care fight — despite the warnings of many of his closest advisers — and how he ended up making deals with many of the powerful special interests he had campaigned against.
